items.title: I can define consciousness and explain why it is a psychological construct
items.what: Consciousness is the level of awareness an individual has of their thoughts, feelings, perceptions, and existence. It is a psychological construct because it cannot be directly observed or measured, but must be inferred from other indicators such as brain wave patterns.
items.why: Defining consciousness correctly establishes the conceptual basis for understanding sleep. Exam questions often test whether students can explain what makes something a psychological construct.
items.example: A researcher cannot directly see whether someone is conscious. Instead, they attach an EEG to measure brain wave patterns and infer the person's level of awareness from those readings.

subtopic.name: Sleep as a Psychological Construct
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces sleep as a psychological construct and a naturally occurring altered state of consciousness. It covers the types of consciousness, the consciousness continuum, and the structure of sleep including REM and NREM stages.
subtopic.why: Understanding what sleep is, and how it differs from waking consciousness, is the foundation for all further study of sleep in VCE Psychology. Exam questions frequently ask students to define sleep precisely and distinguish between its stages.

items.title: I can distinguish between normal waking consciousness (NWC) and altered states of consciousness (ASC)
items.what: Normal waking consciousness (NWC) is a state in which an individual is awake and aware. An altered state of consciousness (ASC) is distinctly different from NWC in terms of quality of experience and levels of awareness.
items.why: This distinction is directly assessed in VCE exams. Students must be able to classify states of consciousness correctly and explain what makes them different.
items.example: A student sitting in class and taking notes is in NWC. The same student falling asleep during class transitions into an ASC, specifically sleep.

subtopic.why: Understanding what sleep is, and how it differs from waking consciousness, is the foundation for all further study of sleep in VCE Psychology. Exam questions frequently ask students to define sleep precisely and distinguish between its stages.

items.title: I can distinguish between naturally occurring and induced altered states of consciousness
items.what: A naturally occurring ASC arises without deliberate intervention, such as sleep or daydreaming. An induced ASC occurs due to a purposeful action or aid, such as meditation, hypnosis, or the influence of alcohol.
items.why: VCE exam questions ask students to categorise specific states of consciousness. Knowing this distinction allows correct classification of sleep as a naturally occurring ASC.
items.example: A person who takes a prescribed sedative to sleep has entered an induced ASC. A person who falls asleep without any substances or techniques has entered a naturally occurring ASC.

subtopic.why: Understanding what sleep is, and how it differs from waking consciousness, is the foundation for all further study of sleep in VCE Psychology. Exam questions frequently ask students to define sleep precisely and distinguish between its stages.

items.title: I can define sleep and explain why it is both a psychological construct and a naturally occurring ASC
items.what: Sleep is a regular and naturally occurring altered state of consciousness that involves a loss of awareness and disengagement with internal and external stimuli. It is a psychological construct because the subjective experience of sleep cannot be overtly measured, yet there is a general agreed understanding of what it is.
items.why: The precise definition of sleep is a common exam target. Students must be able to reproduce and explain this definition, including both its construct and ASC dimensions.
items.example: A person who is asleep is less aware of sounds in the room and loses track of time. A researcher studying them cannot directly observe their subjective experience of sleep, but can infer it from EEG readings.

items.title: I can describe the characteristics of sleep that distinguish it from waking consciousness
items.what: Characteristics of sleep include a reduced ability to control behaviour, reduced control over thoughts, a less accurate sense of time passage, and perceptual and cognitive distortions.
items.why: These characteristics explain how sleep differs qualitatively from NWC and support the classification of sleep as an ASC.
items.example: A sleeping person cannot choose what they dream about (reduced control over thoughts) and may feel as though only minutes passed when they actually slept for several hours (less accurate time perception).

items.title: I can define REM and NREM sleep and identify the key characteristics of each
items.what: REM (rapid eye movement) sleep is characterised by rapid eye movement, high levels of brain activity, and low levels of physical activity due to muscle paralysis. NREM (non-rapid eye movement) sleep is characterised by a lack of rapid eye movement and is subdivided into three stages with progressively deeper sleep.
items.why: Distinguishing REM from NREM sleep is a core skill assessed throughout the chapter. Questions frequently ask students to compare the two types based on specific physiological features.
items.example: During REM sleep, a person's eyes move rapidly beneath their eyelids and they are likely dreaming vividly, but their body is almost completely still. During NREM stage 3, the person is in deep sleep, their body may move slightly, but they are not dreaming vividly.

subtopic.name: Sleep as a Psychological Construct
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces sleep as a psychological construct and a naturally occurring altered state of consciousness. It covers the types of consciousness, the consciousness continuum, and the structure of sleep including REM and NREM stages.
subtopic.why: Understanding what sleep is, and how it differs from waking consciousness, is the foundation for all further study of sleep in VCE Psychology. Exam questions frequently ask students to define sleep precisely and distinguish between its stages.

items.title: I can describe the three stages of NREM sleep and the features that distinguish them
items.what: NREM stage 1 is a light transitional sleep where the sleeper may experience hypnagogic sensations such as a hypnic jerk. NREM stage 2 is a relatively light but true sleep where individuals spend the most time asleep. NREM stage 3 is deep sleep from which it is difficult to wake the sleeper, and in which sleepwalking and sleep talking are most likely.
items.why: NREM stage characteristics are tested directly in apply-and-analyse questions. Students must be able to infer which stage a person is in from a described scenario.
items.example: A student falls asleep on the bus and jolts awake suddenly as if they were falling — this hypnic jerk indicates they were in NREM stage 1. If the same student was later found walking around and was disoriented when woken, they were likely in NREM stage 3.

subtopic.name: Sleep as a Psychological Construct
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces sleep as a psychological construct and a naturally occurring altered state of consciousness. It covers the types of consciousness, the consciousness continuum, and the structure of sleep including REM and NREM stages.
subtopic.why: Understanding what sleep is, and how it differs from waking consciousness, is the foundation for all further study of sleep in VCE Psychology. Exam questions frequently ask students to define sleep precisely and distinguish between its stages.

items.title: I can define a sleep cycle and a sleep episode and describe how they relate to each other
items.what: A sleep episode is the full duration of time spent asleep. A sleep cycle is an approximately 90-minute repeating period within a sleep episode during which an individual progresses through stages of REM and NREM sleep. A typical sleep episode contains around four to five sleep cycles.
items.why: Understanding the relationship between sleep cycles and episodes is needed to interpret hypnograms and answer questions about how sleep architecture changes over a night.
items.example: An adult who sleeps for approximately 7.5 hours will typically complete around five sleep cycles, each roughly 90 minutes long, progressing through NREM stages and REM sleep in each cycle.

subtopic.name: Sleep as a Psychological Construct
subtopic.what: This subtopic introduces sleep as a psychological construct and a naturally occurring altered state of consciousness. It covers the types of consciousness, the consciousness continuum, and the structure of sleep including REM and NREM stages.
subtopic.why: Understanding what sleep is, and how it differs from waking consciousness, is the foundation for all further study of sleep in VCE Psychology. Exam questions frequently ask students to define sleep precisely and distinguish between its stages.

items.title: I can explain the difference between objective physiological measures and subjective measures of sleep
items.what: Objective physiological measures such as EEGs, EMGs, and EOGs provide reliable, quantitative, unbiased data about physical changes during sleep. Subjective measures such as sleep diaries and video monitoring rely on personal experience or interpretation and can provide both qualitative and quantitative data.
items.why: Understanding the objective/subjective distinction is needed for comparison questions and for evaluating the strengths and limitations of each measurement method.
items.example: An EEG objectively records electrical activity in the brain during sleep. A sleep diary in which a person estimates how long they slept and describes how rested they feel is subjective, because it depends on the individual's own perception.

subtopic.name: Measuring Sleep
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the five main methods used to measure sleep: EEG, EMG, EOG, sleep diaries, and video monitoring. It includes how each device works, what it measures, and the brain wave patterns associated with different sleep stages.
subtopic.why: Sleep measurement is directly assessed in VCE exams through recall, application, and data analysis questions. Students must be able to describe each tool precisely, compare objective and subjective measures, and apply their knowledge to novel scenarios.

items.title: I can define an EEG and describe how it is used to measure sleep
items.what: An electroencephalograph (EEG) is a device that detects, amplifies, and records the electrical activity of the brain. Electrodes are attached to the outside of the head to detect electrical impulses from neurons, which are then represented as brain wave patterns that can be used to infer the stage of sleep.
items.why: The EEG is the most frequently examined sleep measurement tool in VCE Psychology. Students must be able to define it precisely, using the phrase 'detects, amplifies, and records' and specifying that it measures electrical activity of the brain.
items.example: During a sleep study, a researcher attaches electrodes to a participant's scalp. While the participant is in NREM stage 3, the EEG shows low-frequency, high-amplitude delta-like brain waves, indicating deep sleep.

subtopic.name: Measuring Sleep
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the five main methods used to measure sleep: EEG, EMG, EOG, sleep diaries, and video monitoring. It includes how each device works, what it measures, and the brain wave patterns associated with different sleep stages.
subtopic.why: Sleep measurement is directly assessed in VCE exams through recall, application, and data analysis questions. Students must be able to describe each tool precisely, compare objective and subjective measures, and apply their knowledge to novel scenarios.

items.title: I can describe the brain wave patterns associated with each stage of sleep as recorded by an EEG
items.what: EEG readings vary in frequency (waves per second) and amplitude (height/intensity) across sleep stages. REM sleep shows high-frequency, low-amplitude beta-like waves. NREM stage 1 shows high-but-reduced frequency and low-but-increased amplitude (alpha-like). NREM stage 2 shows medium frequency and medium-high amplitude (theta-like). NREM stage 3 shows low-frequency, high-amplitude delta-like waves.
items.why: Brain wave patterns are tested in data analysis and application questions. Students must be able to interpret an EEG description and identify the likely sleep stage, or predict what an EEG would show given a described scenario.
items.example: A participant in a sleep lab is found to have low-frequency, high-amplitude brain waves on the EEG. A researcher would infer the participant is in NREM stage 3, the deepest stage of sleep.

subtopic.why: Sleep measurement is directly assessed in VCE exams through recall, application, and data analysis questions. Students must be able to describe each tool precisely, compare objective and subjective measures, and apply their knowledge to novel scenarios.

items.title: I can define an EMG and describe what it shows during REM and NREM sleep
items.what: An electromyograph (EMG) is a device that detects, amplifies, and records the electrical activity of the body's muscles. During REM sleep, an EMG shows low activity due to the near-paralysis of muscles. During NREM sleep, an EMG shows medium or moderate activity, with activity decreasing as NREM stages progress.
items.why: EMG readings are tested in questions asking students to predict or interpret physiological readings for a person in a specific sleep stage.
items.example: A researcher observes that a sleeping participant's EMG is showing very low muscle activity. This is consistent with REM sleep, during which the body is essentially paralysed despite the brain being highly active.

subtopic.why: Sleep measurement is directly assessed in VCE exams through recall, application, and data analysis questions. Students must be able to describe each tool precisely, compare objective and subjective measures, and apply their knowledge to novel scenarios.

items.title: I can define an EOG and describe what it shows during REM and NREM sleep
items.what: An electro-oculograph (EOG) is a device that detects, amplifies, and records the electrical activity of the muscles surrounding the eyes, from which eye movements are inferred. During REM sleep, an EOG shows high activity due to rapid eye movements. During NREM sleep, an EOG shows low activity because rapid eye movement does not occur.
items.why: A common exam error is stating that the EOG measures the electrical activity of the eyes themselves rather than the surrounding muscles. Precision in this definition is directly rewarded in marking.
items.example: A sleep researcher notices the EOG for a participant is showing bursts of high electrical activity. This indicates the participant is in REM sleep and their eyes are moving rapidly beneath their closed eyelids.

items.title: I can describe sleep diaries as a measure of sleep, including their strengths and limitations
items.what: Sleep diaries are a record of self-reported descriptions about sleeping periods, including estimated time spent sleeping and judgements about sleep quality and nature, recorded over a period of time (typically several weeks). They can capture both qualitative information (thoughts, feelings) and quantitative information (hours slept, number of awakenings).
items.why: Sleep diaries appear in application questions where students must identify appropriate measures for a scenario or evaluate a measure's reliability and validity.
items.example: A person completing a sleep diary each morning records that they slept for approximately 6 hours, woke twice in the night, felt anxious before bed, and felt groggy upon waking. This provides rich qualitative detail but may be inaccurate if they misjudged when they fell asleep.

subtopic.name: Measuring Sleep
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the five main methods used to measure sleep: EEG, EMG, EOG, sleep diaries, and video monitoring. It includes how each device works, what it measures, and the brain wave patterns associated with different sleep stages.
subtopic.why: Sleep measurement is directly assessed in VCE exams through recall, application, and data analysis questions. Students must be able to describe each tool precisely, compare objective and subjective measures, and apply their knowledge to novel scenarios.

items.title: I can describe video monitoring as a measure of sleep, including its uses and limitations
items.what: Video monitoring uses camera and audio technologies to record an individual during sleep, tracking sleeping and waking periods, movements, and sounds. It is particularly useful for identifying sleep disorders and can be used alongside physiological measures to validate findings. However, its interpretation is subjective, as observed behaviours such as getting out of bed may be ambiguous.
items.why: Video monitoring is often tested in questions about measuring sleep disorders such as sleepwalking, and in questions asking students to evaluate the accuracy of a sleep measure.
items.example: A sleep specialist uses video monitoring alongside an EMG for a patient suspected of sleepwalking. When the EMG shows muscle activity during what should be deep sleep, the video confirms the patient is physically moving around the room.

items.title: I can define biological rhythms and explain what regulates them
items.what: Biological rhythms are repeated biological processes that are regulated by internal mechanisms. They are cyclical patterns of physiological and behavioural change that occur on a regular basis.
items.why: This definition anchors the distinction between circadian and ultradian rhythms. Understanding that these rhythms are internally regulated is key for questions about what happens when external cues are absent or disrupted.
items.example: Even in the absence of clocks or sunlight, a person's body will still cycle through periods of alertness and sleepiness because their biological rhythms are internally driven.

subtopic.name: Regulation of Sleep-Wake Patterns
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.
subtopic.why: Regulation of sleep-wake patterns is a heavily assessed area of VCE Psychology. Students must be able to trace the pathway from external/internal cues through the SCN to melatonin release, and distinguish between circadian and ultradian rhythms with accurate examples.

items.title: I can define circadian rhythms and identify the sleep-wake cycle as an example
items.what: Circadian rhythms are biological and behavioural changes that occur as part of a cycle lasting around 24 hours. The sleep-wake cycle is a circadian rhythm because it involves biological changes across a 24-hour period as individuals transition between sleep and wakefulness.
items.why: Circadian rhythms and the sleep-wake cycle are central concepts in this lesson and are frequently tested in both short-answer and multiple-choice questions.
items.example: A person who wakes at 7am and becomes sleepy at 11pm is following a circadian rhythm. Their body consistently completes this approximately 24-hour cycle of wakefulness and sleep.

subtopic.name: Regulation of Sleep-Wake Patterns
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.
subtopic.why: Regulation of sleep-wake patterns is a heavily assessed area of VCE Psychology. Students must be able to trace the pathway from external/internal cues through the SCN to melatonin release, and distinguish between circadian and ultradian rhythms with accurate examples.

items.title: I can define ultradian rhythms and identify sleep cycles as an example
items.what: Ultradian rhythms are biological and behavioural changes that occur in a cycle lasting less than 24 hours. Sleep cycles are ultradian rhythms because each approximately 90-minute cycle of REM and NREM sleep repeats multiple times within a single sleep episode.
items.why: Students must be able to correctly classify sleep cycles as ultradian rather than circadian rhythms, and explain why, using precise language about cycle duration.
items.example: A person who sleeps for 7.5 hours experiences approximately five complete sleep cycles. Each cycle lasts around 90 minutes and includes NREM stages 1 to 3 followed by REM sleep, making each cycle an ultradian rhythm.

subtopic.name: Regulation of Sleep-Wake Patterns
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.
subtopic.why: Regulation of sleep-wake patterns is a heavily assessed area of VCE Psychology. Students must be able to trace the pathway from external/internal cues through the SCN to melatonin release, and distinguish between circadian and ultradian rhythms with accurate examples.

items.title: I can describe the location and function of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)
items.what: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) is an area of the hypothalamus located above the optic chiasm, made up of approximately 20,000 neurons across two nuclei. It acts as an internal biological clock and regulates the sleep-wake cycle by receiving both external cues (such as light) and internal cues (such as clock genes) and sending signals to the pineal gland.
items.why: The SCN is a key structure in VCE Psychology. Students must accurately describe its location, its inputs, and its output (signalling to the pineal gland), and avoid the common error of stating that the SCN releases melatonin.
items.example: As daylight fades in the evening, the SCN detects reduced light input via the optic chiasm and begins sending neural signals to the pineal gland to begin releasing melatonin.

subtopic.name: Regulation of Sleep-Wake Patterns
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.
subtopic.why: Regulation of sleep-wake patterns is a heavily assessed area of VCE Psychology. Students must be able to trace the pathway from external/internal cues through the SCN to melatonin release, and distinguish between circadian and ultradian rhythms with accurate examples.

items.title: I can describe the role of melatonin in regulating the sleep-wake cycle
items.what: Melatonin is a hormone released by the pineal gland at night-time that promotes feelings of calm and relaxation, thereby facilitating sleep. Melatonin levels begin rising at around 8 to 9pm, peak between 2 and 4am, and gradually decline toward morning. Melatonin does not directly cause sleep but creates the conditions that make falling asleep easier.
items.why: Melatonin is frequently examined. Students must describe it as a hormone released by the pineal gland (not the SCN), and explain that it promotes calm rather than directly inducing sleep.
items.example: At 9pm, a person begins to feel drowsy as melatonin levels in their bloodstream rise. By 2am, melatonin peaks and they are in their deepest sleep. By 6am, melatonin has declined and they wake feeling alert.

subtopic.name: Regulation of Sleep-Wake Patterns
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.
subtopic.why: Regulation of sleep-wake patterns is a heavily assessed area of VCE Psychology. Students must be able to trace the pathway from external/internal cues through the SCN to melatonin release, and distinguish between circadian and ultradian rhythms with accurate examples.

items.title: I can trace the sequence of events by which the SCN regulates sleep through melatonin release
items.what: The SCN receives external cues (such as light levels) and internal cues (such as clock gene activity). It then sends neural messages to the pineal gland, which releases melatonin into the bloodstream. Melatonin promotes relaxation and sleepiness, regulating the timing of sleep in the sleep-wake cycle.
items.why: Extended response and short-answer questions often ask students to explain this process as a sequence. Using accurate terminology and the correct pathway — external/internal cues to SCN to pineal gland to melatonin to sleep — is essential.
items.example: As a student turns off their lamp at night, reduced light reaches the SCN via the optic chiasm. The SCN signals the pineal gland, which releases melatonin into the bloodstream. The student begins to feel calm and sleepy approximately 1 to 2 hours later.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.
subtopic.why: Regulation of sleep-wake patterns is a heavily assessed area of VCE Psychology. Students must be able to trace the pathway from external/internal cues through the SCN to melatonin release, and distinguish between circadian and ultradian rhythms with accurate examples.

items.title: I can describe the role of cortisol in the sleep-wake cycle and contrast it with melatonin
items.what: Cortisol is a hormone released by the adrenal cortex in the morning that increases alertness and maintains heightened arousal, promoting wakefulness. Unlike melatonin (which is high at night and low in the morning), cortisol is high in the morning and low at night. The SCN does not release cortisol.
items.why: Contrast questions comparing cortisol and melatonin, or cortisol and its role in the stress response versus the sleep-wake cycle, appear in exam questions from multiple lessons.
items.example: At 7am, as melatonin levels drop, the adrenal cortex releases cortisol into the bloodstream. A person wakes feeling alert and ready to engage in their morning routine, partly because cortisol is raising their level of arousal.

subtopic.what: This subtopic covers the biological mechanisms that regulate the sleep-wake cycle, including circadian and ultradian rhythms, the role of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), and the hormones melatonin and cortisol.

items.title: I can describe the overall trends in sleep duration and REM proportion across the lifespan
items.what: As age increases, total sleep duration generally decreases and the proportion of REM sleep also generally decreases, though the rate of change in REM proportion slows significantly from childhood onwards. From adolescence through to old age, the proportion of REM sleep stabilises at approximately 20% of a sleep episode.
items.why: Understanding these general trends allows students to answer broad comparison questions and interpret unfamiliar hypnograms by applying the expected patterns for different age groups.
items.example: A newborn sleeps approximately 16 hours with roughly 50% REM sleep. A healthy adult sleeps approximately 7.75 hours with roughly 20% REM sleep — a significant decrease in both duration and REM proportion across the lifespan.

subtopic.name: Sleep Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how sleep duration, proportion of REM and NREM sleep, and sleep onset patterns change from the neonatal period through to old age, along with explanations for why these changes occur.
subtopic.why: Sleep across the lifespan is directly assessed through comparison questions, hypnogram interpretation, and extended responses. Students must be able to describe trends, compare age groups, and explain differences with reference to brain development and physiological needs.

items.title: I can describe the sleep characteristics of the neonatal period and explain why REM sleep is so high
items.what: During the neonatal period (1 to 15 days), sleep duration is at its highest in the lifespan at approximately 16 hours. Approximately 50% of the sleep episode is REM sleep and 50% is NREM sleep. The high proportion of REM sleep is explained by the rapid brain development occurring during this period.
items.why: The neonatal period provides the most extreme contrast with adult sleep and is a common reference point in comparison questions and hypnogram tasks.
items.example: A two-day-old baby sleeping for 16 hours will spend approximately 8 of those hours in REM sleep. This high proportion of REM reflects the intense neural development occurring in the newborn brain.

subtopic.name: Sleep Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how sleep duration, proportion of REM and NREM sleep, and sleep onset patterns change from the neonatal period through to old age, along with explanations for why these changes occur.
subtopic.why: Sleep across the lifespan is directly assessed through comparison questions, hypnogram interpretation, and extended responses. Students must be able to describe trends, compare age groups, and explain differences with reference to brain development and physiological needs.

items.title: I can describe how sleep changes from infancy through childhood and explain the reduction in REM sleep
items.what: During infancy (3 to 24 months), sleep duration decreases to approximately 13.5 hours and the proportion of REM sleep drops to approximately 35%, with NREM increasing to approximately 65%. Through childhood (2 to 14 years), sleep duration decreases further to approximately 11 hours and REM proportion drops to around 20%, with NREM around 80%. This reflects the steadying of the pace of brain development.
items.why: Childhood and infancy represent significant transition points in the lifespan data. Students are often asked to compare these periods or explain why REM sleep decreases during these years.
items.example: A 3-year-old sleeping 12 hours may spend approximately 25% of that time (3 hours) in REM sleep. A 13-year-old sleeping 10 hours may spend approximately 18.5% (about 1.75 hours) in REM sleep — a decline reflecting slower brain development.

subtopic.name: Sleep Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how sleep duration, proportion of REM and NREM sleep, and sleep onset patterns change from the neonatal period through to old age, along with explanations for why these changes occur.
subtopic.why: Sleep across the lifespan is directly assessed through comparison questions, hypnogram interpretation, and extended responses. Students must be able to describe trends, compare age groups, and explain differences with reference to brain development and physiological needs.

items.title: I can describe the sleep characteristics of adolescence, including delayed sleep onset
items.what: Adolescents (14 to 18 years) typically sleep approximately 9 hours, with roughly 20% REM and 80% NREM sleep. A key feature of adolescent sleep is a biologically driven delayed sleep onset of 1 to 2 hours, meaning adolescents naturally become sleepier later and wake later than adults. Social factors such as early school start times and evening social commitments also reduce total sleep in this group.
items.why: The delayed sleep onset in adolescence is a specific and examinable feature. Students must be able to attribute it to biological mechanisms (delayed circadian phase) rather than purely behavioural choices.
items.example: A Year 11 student naturally does not feel sleepy until midnight due to a biologically delayed circadian phase. Because school starts at 8:30am, they accumulate a sleep deficit across the week, which is a form of partial sleep deprivation.

subtopic.name: Sleep Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how sleep duration, proportion of REM and NREM sleep, and sleep onset patterns change from the neonatal period through to old age, along with explanations for why these changes occur.
subtopic.why: Sleep across the lifespan is directly assessed through comparison questions, hypnogram interpretation, and extended responses. Students must be able to describe trends, compare age groups, and explain differences with reference to brain development and physiological needs.

items.title: I can describe how sleep changes from young adulthood through to middle adulthood
items.what: Young adults (18 to 30 years) sleep approximately 7.75 hours, with 20% REM and 80% NREM sleep. During middle adulthood (30 to 75 years), sleep duration remains relatively stable at approximately 7 to 8 hours and the REM/NREM proportion remains constant. Sleep patterns in adulthood are the most stable phase of the lifespan.
items.why: Adulthood represents the stable baseline against which other lifespan stages are compared. Students should be able to describe it accurately and use it as a reference point in extended comparison questions.
items.example: A healthy 35-year-old sleeping 7.5 hours will typically cycle through approximately five 90-minute sleep cycles, spending roughly 20% of that time (about 1.5 hours) in REM sleep across the night.

subtopic.name: Sleep Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how sleep duration, proportion of REM and NREM sleep, and sleep onset patterns change from the neonatal period through to old age, along with explanations for why these changes occur.
subtopic.why: Sleep across the lifespan is directly assessed through comparison questions, hypnogram interpretation, and extended responses. Students must be able to describe trends, compare age groups, and explain differences with reference to brain development and physiological needs.

items.title: I can describe the sleep characteristics of old age, including advanced sleep phase and increased awakenings
items.what: Older adults (75 years and above) typically sleep approximately 6 hours, still with approximately 20% REM and 80% NREM sleep. They tend to experience advanced sleep phase syndrome, a biological shift that causes them to feel sleepy earlier and wake earlier. Older adults also experience increased brief awakenings during the sleep episode.
items.why: Old age sleep features — particularly advanced sleep phase and increased awakenings — are assessed in hypnogram interpretation tasks and comparison questions with other age groups.
items.example: A 78-year-old who consistently feels ready for sleep at 8pm and wakes at 4am is exhibiting advanced sleep phase syndrome. A hypnogram of their sleep would show multiple brief returns to wakefulness across the night, unlike a typical adult hypnogram.

subtopic.name: Sleep Across the Lifespan
subtopic.what: This subtopic covers how sleep duration, proportion of REM and NREM sleep, and sleep onset patterns change from the neonatal period through to old age, along with explanations for why these changes occur.
subtopic.why: Sleep across the lifespan is directly assessed through comparison questions, hypnogram interpretation, and extended responses. Students must be able to describe trends, compare age groups, and explain differences with reference to brain development and physiological needs.

items.title: I can explain why sleep demands differ across the lifespan with reference to brain development and physiological needs
items.what: REM sleep is associated with brain and cognitive development and rest, while NREM sleep is associated with physiological rest and development. High REM sleep demands in infancy and early childhood reflect rapid brain development. As development slows through childhood and into adulthood, REM requirements decrease. Reduced sleep in older adults relates to decreased cognitive and physical growth, and to increased prevalence of sleep disorders and ill-health.
items.why: Explanation questions asking students to justify why sleep changes across the lifespan are common in extended response tasks. Students must link sleep type (REM or NREM) to a specific biological function.
items.example: A newborn needs approximately 50% REM sleep because its brain is forming billions of new neural connections. A healthy adult needs only 20% REM sleep because the rate of brain development has slowed dramatically since infancy.

items.title: I can compare the sleep requirements and typical sleep averages across the lifespan and explain any discrepancies
items.what: Sleep requirements refer to the amount of sleep needed for healthy functioning, while sleep averages refer to how much people typically actually sleep. These do not always match. For example, older adults require 7 to 8 hours but typically average only 6 hours, and adolescents require 8 to 10 hours but average around 9 hours. Discrepancies arise from social, environmental, and health factors.
items.why: VCE questions use the term 'demands' for sleep requirements. Understanding the distinction between requirements and averages, and explaining gaps between them, is needed for high-level application responses.
items.example: A 16-year-old requires 8 to 10 hours of sleep but averages 7.5 hours due to homework demands and early school start times. This 0.5 to 2.5 hour shortfall represents ongoing partial sleep deprivation despite the student sleeping every night.
